newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-Allied Carpets see consumer demand.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Allied Carpets see consumer demand.

text.p: British carpet retailer Allied Carpets Plc on Monday reported a 15 percent increase in annual profits, despite a second half slump in sales in the run-up to the UK General Election.

And in the six weeks since the middle of June, like-for-like sales have grown 14 percent as cash windfalls from the flotation of building societies, an improving housing market and a catch-up from the second half "malaise" boosted consumer confidence.
"The thing that runs through all this is just improving consumer confidence," managing director Ray Nethercott said in a telephone conference call.
"(But) this business is about long-term strategy, it's not about election blips, it's not about windfall gains," he said.
The company, which floated on the stock market in July 1996, reported a 15 percent jump in pre-tax profit to 16.7 million stg for the year to June 28 and total dividend of 7.5 pence a share.
"What the business has demonstrated is its ability to grow its profit in difficult trading conditions," said Nethercott.

Like-for-like sales grew by 13 percent in the first half but slumped by five percent in the second six months as uncertainty surrounding the May 1 General Election resulted in a sharp 12 percent drop in like for like sales in March, April and May.
"I don't think anybody...expected that the pre-election blip was going to as serious as it was, for as long as was," he said.
The carpet market as a whole was also volatile in the year, growing six percent in the first half but dropping an estimated 10 percent in the second six months, he added.
Allied's market share increased by 2.0 percent in the year to 14 percent, although in the same period it saw its key rival Carpetright Plc boost its share from 13 to 17 percent.
Finance director David Pout agreed Carpetright has a larger market share, but said with planned store openings this year "I think we'll see ourselves catching up as we move forward now."
The company plans to open a minimum 20 Allied stores, which target the middle to upper market segment, and 15-20 Carpetland stores, which target the lower end, this year.
Last year it opened a record 36 stores for a total of 238 -- 212 Allied and 26 Carpetland. Pout said it was "proceeding well" in its medium target of 300 Allied and 100 Carpetland stores.
Orders of more than 1,000 stg grew twice the overall growth rate last year and now accounts for 40 percent of its business.
"This is where we see ourselves continuing to penetrate in the coming year, the mid to upper segment of the market," Pout added.

Nethercott said Allied hoped to steal a march on its competitors when its rolls out it HomeVision system -- an imaging system which enables customers to view any carpet they select on a large screen -- at its stores in September 13.
Trials had already been held in 10 stores had proved "very, very successful," he said.
Netercott added that while discretionary spending from the windfalls gains was a "big chunk of money" he thought customers would continue to seek value and not rush to buy.
"I reckon we're going to see the benefits of the windfall gains spread over the next six months at least".
